lines.text: Facial expressions are the most immediate and universal form of nonverbal communication. A smile can convey warmth, politeness, amusement, or even discomfort — context determines the meaning. A genuine smile, known as a Duchenne smile, engages both the mouth and the eyes, creating crow's feet at the outer corners. A forced or polite smile only moves the lips. A frown — the downward pull of the eyebrows and mouth corners — signals displeasure, concentration, or confusion. Raised eyebrows indicate surprise, scepticism, or an invitation to continue speaking. A furrowed brow shows deep thought, worry, or frustration. Eye contact varies culturally: in Western business settings, steady eye contact shows confidence and honesty, while avoiding eye contact may suggest shyness, dishonesty, or — in many Asian and Middle Eastern cultures — respect for authority. A smirk, the one-sided half-smile, often communicates smugness, sarcasm, or quiet amusement. Pursed lips suggest disapproval or careful thought. A clenched jaw reveals tension, anger, or determination. Blushing — the involuntary reddening of the cheeks — signals embarrassment, shame, or sometimes attraction. Tears can express sadness, joy, frustration, or relief. Yawning, while physiological, is often read as boredom or fatigue. Understanding these expressions helps language learners decode unspoken messages and respond appropriately in conversation.

lines.text: In English-speaking cultures, smiling at strangers is common — in shops, on the street, at bus stops. This 'social smile' is politeness, not genuine happiness. Not smiling back can be perceived as unfriendly, even rude. This differs from many European and Asian cultures.
lines.name: In English-speaking cultures, smiling at strangers is common — in shops, on the street, at bus stops. This 'social smile' is politeness, not genuine happiness. Not smiling back can be perceived as unfriendly, even rude. This differs from many European and Asian cultures.

lines.text: In British and American culture, moderate eye contact shows engagement. Too much can feel aggressive; too little suggests dishonesty or shyness. In many Middle Eastern and East Asian cultures, lowering the gaze shows respect. Context is everything.

lines.text: 'Resting face' (sometimes called 'resting serious face') is when someone's neutral expression looks unfriendly. English speakers are very aware of this concept — it's discussed openly and even humorously. Understanding this prevents misreading someone's mood.

lines.text: Remote work has made facial expressions even more important. English speakers consciously manage their expressions on camera — nodding, smiling, and reacting visibly to show engagement. A blank screen face is often misread as disinterest.

lines.text: Psychology research shows 'micro-expressions' — fleeting facial movements lasting fractions of a second — reveal true emotions. Words like 'flicker' (a flicker of doubt crossed her face), 'flash' (a flash of anger), and 'shadow' (a shadow of sadness) describe these brief expressions.
